blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
[DR A] (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
[Dr A], could you restate your full name for the recording, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr A], you've been invited to return to give evidence in relation to your involvement with the patient [Baby Q] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and in particular, as to the events of 25 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Have you had the opportunity to refresh your memory from the clinical notes made about [Baby Q] during his time at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I have, thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Do you have a working memory of your involvement with [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I have more memory about the following day, but having looked at the notes, I'm aware of what was happening on the 25th.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we please go, Mr Murphy, to our tile 103 and the clinical notes that underpin it, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Towards the bottom of this first page, is that your handwriting we see at 09.17 hours on 25 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. The first line of which bears the letters WR, does that indicate ward round?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the next line reads, am I right:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Called to NNU at 09.17 because of desaturation"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To read those words literally would imply that you were not in the NNU at 09.17; is that right or wrong?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It looks as though I was not there at 9.17, I may have been on the children's ward, we may have still been doing the handover from the night team.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you have any memory as to how you were called to the NNU at 09.17?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you please consider the next part of the note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does the second line continue to explain why you were called to the NNU?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what do these next few lines inform the reader of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "Had just vomited and then desaturated to the low 60s, minor bradycardia. Bagged with a Neopuff circuit on a pressure of 20/5 in 100% oxygen. Soon returned to 100% [that'll be the saturations]."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we pause there and can you assist the jury to understand which, if any, of those few sentences you read out are derived from your direct observations and which represent information conveyed to you by somebody else at the NNU?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Okay. It doesn't state whether it's myself or somebody else. The fact that I used the past tense, I would imagine that [Baby Q] has already vomited and then had a desaturation. "Bagged up in 100% oxygen", I would imagine I was there at that point but not necessarily.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you recall from whom you received the information that he had desaturated, just vomited and was in the low 60s?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, I'm afraid I don't. It may have been a bleep, in which case it will have been whoever made the phone call.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Taking a step back from 09.17 on 25 June for a moment, do you recall that a day or two later [Baby Q] was transferred from Chester to Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And do you recall being involved in that transfer and in the documentation that went with him --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- to Alder Hey? We'll return to this note in a moment, but just dealing with that, could we go to tile 310, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There is a transfer letter penned by you and a colleague, I believe. If we could go down that page -- continue down, please, Mr Murphy -- to a section that is entitled "GI/hepatic".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr A], can you tell the jury what the purpose of this paragraph was in this context within the transfer letter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So the system that produces these letters gives you preformatted headers, such as haematological and GI/hepatic, and it gives you a pertinent place to record those details for each baby who's being transferred.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. In this context what do the letters GI stand for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Gastrointestinal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see that in the middle of this entry, under the "GI/hepatic", you make reference to the morning of 25 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's been described here as:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Profuse vomit with desaturation on morning of 25 June."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were they your words?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: They are my words, but they will have been taken from the recording made of that vomit, which may well be an observation by whoever was looking after [Baby Q] on that day.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go back then to our tile 103 and your clinical notes. You had kindly taken us down as far as the recording of the fact that he'd been bagged via the Neopuff. What was the consequence of that bagging?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: His oxygen saturations returned to 100%, which was ideal, but unfortunately [Baby Q] then continued to have a requirement for PEEP, so it's a little bit of back pressure just to hold the lungs open at the end of a breath, and because of that, he was moved from, I presume, nursery 2 or 3 towards nursery 1, and then started on CPAP, which delivers the same pressure of air but in a more formal way.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That requirement for PEEP, for that positive endexpiratory pressure, I think it stands for --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- were you able to discern whether that was indicative of the cause of his problems or whether it was the consequence of the earlier problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At that time, no, it was a requirement and whether that was the reason for the vomit or whether it was a consequence of it is impossible to tell, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you recorded his movement to nursery 1 because of this requirement?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then you considered other features of the baby; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the next feature that you considered?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He has an umbilical venous catheter in situ and therefore he was re-screened and commenced on teicoplanin and cefotaxime, which were, in Chester at the time, the antibiotics for use in case of a line infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So taking a step back from that, he was about 4 days old at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the UVC in situ, had that been in situ from day 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I suspect so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At this point, 09.17 on 25 June, was there anything indicative of an infection at or around the UVC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Therefore was this a precautionary prescription on your part?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So this UVC is a long length of indwelling plastic and it is a risk, it takes a direct route into one of the central veins, and I would rather start [Baby Q] on antibiotics and stop
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: when I know that he doesn't need them than not start and be too late.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that an established potential for infection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And therefore an established precautionary response?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you please, Mr Murphy, take us to the next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What does this show?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So I will have placed a cannula at this point and the blood tests that are recorded on the end of the previous page will have been taken. One of those, because there was venous blood available, was a venous gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. There is a file in front of you, the one at the top has a number 2 on the spine. Behind divider 22 there's a small bundle of documents from [Baby Q]'s file, as it were, and it's variously paginated but in the top right corner there's a three-digit pagination stamp. Could you please go to page 008?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If you could look, firstly, please, at the entries for the morning of 25 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see at 06.58, at a point in time when [Baby Q] was self-ventilating in air, there was a blood gas taken, measured and recorded. Are you able to evaluate those readings, [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. This is a very acceptable gas for a baby of 31 weeks and 4 days. A pH of 7.296 is ideal. A CO2 of 6.86, looking at the trend of those, is not changing very much. The oxygen from a capillary gas, we don't really look at. The bicarbonate is normal. The base excess is a little bit above what I would like it to be, but it's only changed a little from the previous gas from the evening of the 24th. Blood glucose and blood lactate are normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So that's at 06.58, which is the last reading prior to the episode about which you were called to the NNU to care and examine [Baby Q]. The next we see is timed at 09.56. What can you tell us about that reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This is the gas that is recorded in my notes as venous on this chart. It has a C in it, which would suggest capillary. I suspect that that's been recorded wrongly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So do you, by that, suggest that you prefer your note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think that to have stated that it was a venous gas, with having taken a blood culture at the same time which has to be venous blood, I think that this was a venous gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Can you evaluate that gas?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This is markedly or different to the previous gas at 06.58. The pH is lower, the carbon dioxide is higher, so this is a respiratory acidosis. The bicarbonate is much the same. The base excess has increased to minus 6 from minus 2.8. The blood glucose is acceptable, but again the lactate has increased from 1.2 to 4.0.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So before we move away from the blood gas record chart, in addition to the data you just looked at, there is under the column "type", the record-maker, presumably the nurse, records that prior to the vomit he was self-ventilating in air, but as you've told us, thereafter he received respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we focus on the screen then, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a continuation of the note that you timed at 09.17, but as we look at the next entry, is there a further time noted within there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Underneath the date at the top left, it just says "continued". And it is likely that I will have gone to [Baby Q] at 09.17 and not left him, having just continued my initial assessment of him, the intervention of taking the bloods and the gas, and then I start on the formal ward round review, which he would be due to have that morning anyway.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Below the venous gas data, you've recorded that sodium chloride was provided to [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And do you time --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that at 10.10 is a record of a timed event?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It follows, therefore, that everything thereafter must be --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Is 10.10 and beyond, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So is this now then part of your ward round review of [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: If the preceding events hadn't happened, this would be where I'd normally have started.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Understood. So you begin, as we see from your notes in relation to other patients, by stating his age, gestational age and the like. Does the next line represent some of his history?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you help us with the next two lines after the reference to the placenta, which is something to do with [Baby Q]'s attachment to his mother?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right. So placenta previa and accreta were the reason, we presume, for his early delivery.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: His next line is jaundice with a bilirubin of 220, which at 31 weeks of gestation will have required treatment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We've presumed secondary sepsis and then I move on to his ventilation review.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: May I ask what's the basis of that presumption?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So this refers to the notes that are written prior to 10.10, that he's had a vomit and a desaturation and with a UVC in situ, I am treating for presumed infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next entries come alongside the letter V; is this ventilation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you there detail the ventilatory regime that you set him on because of the earlier desaturation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In summary, could you tell us what that records?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So he's receiving CPAP, so continuous positive airway pressure, with a peak end-expiratory pressure of 6 centimetres of water, and that's set on the machine.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the residual pressure that [Baby Q]'s lungs are inflated to at the end of a breath. His oxygen requirement being delivered through the machine is 25%, and I have commented that his nasal septum is intact.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby Q]'s oxygen saturations are 99% in 25% of oxygen and his heart rate is now 160 beats per minute, having had a bolus at 10.10. They were previously between 190 and 200. His respiratory rate is still elevated at 70 to 80 breaths per minute.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Comparatively, comparing events after 10 -his presentation, forgive me, after 10.10 as compared to 09.17, how was he after the passage of an hour or so?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: With that bolus of sodium chloride being given, I've managed to reduce his heart rate, so he's not having to work as hard to pump blood around because the volume in his venous system is increased.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And in terms of his general stability?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He's no longer needing 100% oxygen through a Neopuff, he's only needing 25%, and in that he has oxygen saturations of 99%.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If Mr Murphy could take us down the page, please. F, is that feeding?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Feeds and fluids.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was the regime as dictated by you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So at this moment in time he is nil by mouth and he is receiving IV fluids, which are the parenteral nutrition fluids stored in a fridge on the unit, and he is receiving Babiven Start-up, which is the proprietary name for one of the electrolyte solutions, it contains the salts. He is receiving 9ml per hour and the lipid component of his parenteral nutrition is a brand name called SMOF, and he is receiving 1.29ml per hour of that to give him a total fluid volume of 120ml per kilo per day.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. He passed urine, the notes suggest?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then did you record his presentation upon examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. That's the next few lines.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You record that he was settled, which speaks for itself.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did he have a rosy appearance, but was also a bit yellow?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Both of those at the same time, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. You record that he was under phototherapy for the jaundice, we presume, is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He is and his treatment line at day 4 of life is 210.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I recall from the transfer letter that you showed me just now that his bilirubin had been at 220 and we would only normally stop or reduce the phototherapy when the patient is 50 below the treatment line.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. The next two entries, can you take those together, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. His heart sounds are 1 plus 2 plus 0, which are normal heart sounds in neonates and children and adults. His femoral pulses were palpable on both sides of his groin. His peripheral perfusion was better since he'd received that bolus of 10ml per kilo. And his blood pressure is 69/37mmHg, and his mean arterial pressure is 50. That will have been recorded on the machine that measures the blood pressure at the incubator side. His chest is clear, there are no additional sounds at this time, his abdomen is soft and non-tender, his umbilicus looks normal, there's no flare or redness around it, and his anterior fontanelle is soft, his tone and movements are normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In the absence of a flare around the UVC, is there any significance that can be attached to the absence of that finding?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So if there is a flare or redness around the umbilicus, that suggests that there is an infection of the skin at that point and because there is then an open route down into the abdomen through the umbilical cord, it's taken as a significant finding. In this instance there was no flare, there was no redness and his abdomen was soft at that time. These were reassuring things, but he still had the UVC in situ.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Understood. But redness or a flare would be something that would tend to confirm infection in --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- or around the UVC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So having thoroughly examined him and recorded the pertinent features of that examination, what was your general impression as recorded towards the bottom of the screen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The first line is:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Presumed sepsis with secondary jaundice."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I'm recording that -- jaundice can increase during infection, it's an associated sign. Then line 2 is:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Poor gas, [query] aspiration."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that refers to the large vomit and subsequent desaturation down to the 60s, requiring now CPAP.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we pause there and expand upon that a little if you would?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The poor gas, is that the reading at 09.56 that we looked at on the chart?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So, "[Question]..." -- does that say "aspirant"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "Aspiration."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So what is it that you're noting there, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I'm raising the query that following that large vomit, [Baby Q] may have inhaled some of the vomitus into his chest, which was responsible for the poor gas and may then lead on to infection in subsequent hours and days.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you're noting and raising the possibility that the readings may be the consequence of the vomit as opposed to the cause?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So your plan of action?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Start IV cefotaxime and IV teicoplanin. A gas 1 hour after starting CPAP. Chest X-ray. May need metronidazole if evidence of aspiration."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's see how that plan was put into effect, please, in part, if we go to tile 131. Part of your plan was for a further blood gas to be taken in about an hour's time; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that where we are now? We see that collected at 11.21 that morning, so about an hour later.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I suspect that the samples were requested earlier than 11.21 because they'd been received in the laboratory at the same time they were collected and that can't be the case.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from the note we've just read that that was post 10.10?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. It was around about 10.10 because he will have had the bolus, the blood culture and gas, and the other bloods that I listed there will have been collected at the same time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that note included a plan for a gas in a hour hence --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we won't get hung up on the precise time that the gas was taken. More importantly, what do the results inform you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: On this top set of results, this is his biochemistry readings, his sodium is normal, his potassium is normal, his bicarbonate is a little low, it's just a shade under the reference range, his urea is high, his creatine is at the top end of normal, and his bilirubin is 146, again that would then be referenced to the bilirubin treatment charts which are gestational age specific.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. What conclusions can be safely drawn from those results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Biochemically, [Baby Q] is a little dry at the moment, he needs more fluid. That may well have been partly responsible for his increased heart rate in the 190-200 range that we have discussed just now.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What, if anything, does it inform you of, of the causal relationship vis-à-vis the vomit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It doesn't give me an explanation of why it is, it just tells me what it is and then from that I draw conclusions and then make a treatment plan.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. If we just look at the paper document, the blood gas record, we can see that there was a gas taken at 11.12 according to the paper document.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that this reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, the results that are here are the biochemistry and haematology results. The blood gas will have been done locally within the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Understood. But whilst we're on that row, could you evaluate those blood gas readings from 11.12?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. His pH has normalised and it's better than the reading at 6.58 that morning. His carbon dioxide has come down to an acceptable level because of that peak end-expiratory pressure that's allowing him to blow off more carbon dioxide. Oxygen, again, is not really commented on on a capillary or venous gas. His bicarbonate has changed slightly but not much. His base excess has halved in the time since the bolus and the CPAP started and, by the look of this record, he is no longer in 25% oxygen but down to 21%. His glucose is very slightly increased but his lactate has come down nicely and is pretty much the same as it was at 6.58 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We know that another feature of your plan was the suggestion that an X-ray should be taken.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go to tile 135, we see an X-ray timestamped at 11.52 that morning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down to, please, consider the analysis of it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What does that X-ray tell you and how does that inform your assessment of the vomit and desaturation that was the reason why you were called to him in the first place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So the second half of this report is the bit that's pertinent to his chest. There is mild interstitial shadowing with a trace of fluid in the horizontal fissure. There is no focal collapse or consolidation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this doesn't suggest that there is a large amount of foreign matter in his lungs, it doesn't suggest that he's had or is evolving a chest infection. The reason for doing the chest X-ray is to see whether those things are there at that time and are responsible for the collapse and it appears not.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. I think there's a later X-ray at tile 163. We'll look at that while we're considering the X-rays -- no, I think this is just your note then of the consideration of that. But let's click on here, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So did you return to see [Baby Q] at 13.50?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I've recorded the chest X-ray and the blood test results and then I've documented a plan. It looks as though I have signed off there, so I may or may not have examined him. I suspect not if I've not recorded it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So is this a note of your consideration of the chest Xray we've just looked at and the earlier blood results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. And the plan was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: To increase the fluids and we can go a day ahead. So instead of remaining on 120ml per kilo per day -- to go up to 150ml per kilo per day.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that because of features within those blood analysis which led you to think, in simple terms, he needed more fluids?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There's three numbers there that have made that my plan: it's the urea being elevated at 7.9, the creatine being just at the top end of that reference range, 70, and the haematocrit, which is a measure of concentration of cells within the blood is on -- it's not very high but I would prefer it in the 0.3 range and giving extra fluids will reduce that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the white blood cells evaluation or is that something different?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, so the white cell count listed here is 7.4. Of the white cells, I then go on to document the neutrophils and the lymphocytes, which are -- they've got different roles in fighting infection. His platelets here are a little bit low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, that is a suggestion of infection or bleeding. The haematocrit is a measure of concentration and [Baby Q]'s blood here is a little bit more concentrated. That supports the fact that his urea is slightly raised. By giving more fluid, the urea number will come down as a waste product and the amount of concentration of cells within his blood will settle.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In summary, how did you assess the white blood cell readings?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The white cell count is not significantly raised but this is all within an hour or two of his initial deterioration. This white cell count number reflects what's going on at the time of taking the sample, it doesn't tell you what response [Baby Q] would have had from that -- or from an infection developing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it capable of informing you of cause or effect?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The trend of the neutrophils and the lymphocytes are recorded there as NX and LX: if the neutrophil count goes up, that suggests bacterial infection; if the lymphocyte count goes up, that suggests a viral infection. These are both perfectly normal at this time. But the platelet count is something to keep an eye on: I would normally expect that to be in the sort of 140s/150s.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go down the page, Mr Murphy, we can see a further entry, again your handwriting, at 19.20.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which records gases taken at 18.22 which peculiarly, I don't think, appear on the blood gas record, unless I'm mistaken.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, they don't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm not aware of any other document that evidences that particular reading, I stand to be corrected, but plainly, you've obtained this data from somewhere.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: If it's not recorded in the chart that you have provided here, the blood gas machine produces a paper slip and it's that that's taken back to fill in this chart.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I suspect I will have seen that that paper clip was clipped on. There's bulldog clips across the top of the recording chart and I presume I've read it from there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We've heard previously a paper slip referred to as something vaguely resembling a till roll (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Essentially, it is very similar, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that what you're referring to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How are the gases at 18.22?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This is an acceptable gas. The pH of 7.289 is down a little from the one at 4.20. The carbon dioxide is up a little. Base excess again has increased a little.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Glucose is normal. The lactate has continued to stay around about 1.2/1.3.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you comment on the pH level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The pH -- no, I possibly didn't. It is an acceptable pH for a baby on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look at the paper document, how does it compare to the previous pH?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Compared to the one at 16.18, it is down a little but not much.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. The next part of your 19.20 note, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So on review, respiratory rate is trending down with the respiratory rate currently 18 to 20 breaths per minute, starting to look tired, which then clarifies some of the points from that gas. If the respiratory rate is trending down, [Baby Q] will not have as many breaths in which to expel carbon dioxide, so he will be retaining it, which is why the PCO2 there is 6.72, whereas it was 5.95 2 hours ago.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Looking tired whilst being on CPAP suggests that there's a lot of effort being put into breathing and if he is looking tired with results that are starting to turn towards a more respiratory acidosis, then it's time to intervene.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And if we look at the page beneath, we'll see your intervention. If Mr Murphy could take us down. For the reasons that you have just explained to the jury, did you deem it appropriate to discuss the position with Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I did.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was your joint conclusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have explained my observations of [Baby Q]'s breathing and this most recent blood gas result and with [Baby Q] looking to me as though he's tiring, it's the decision to intubate him now rather than wait for him to have a respiratory collapse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So negative indicators and intubate before he tires further, if indeed that was his direction of travel?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you and Dr Gibbs, having arrived at that joint decision, did you share it with [Baby Q]'s parents?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I've recorded here:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Discussed with parents."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And this was performed -- I probably mean "undertaken". I discussed this with his parents prior to his intubation and explained the clinical grounds, why it's necessary to intubate and ventilate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Then does the next entry set out the intubation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It does. I'm listing the intubation -- the pre-intubation drugs given at the time of intubation and then the size of tube and the length to which it's secured.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In summary, was that just a normal intubation process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I see here I've placed that tube on the first attempt and I've put a tick next to capnograph, suggesting that there was normal colour change on it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can Mr Murphy take us further down the page then, please? What was the plan hereafter, post-intubation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So he's been connected to the ventilator and the mode of ventilation is continuous mandatory ventilation, so this is going to deliver breaths for the rate that is set, not measuring [Baby Q]'s effort of breathing. The inspiratory pressure is set at 18 centimetres of water, the PEEP is set at 5 centimetres of water. He is in the same oxygen concentration through the ventilator as room air and the inspiratory phase or the part of the breathing cycle is set at 0.4. That means that the expiratory phase is -- the out-breath is longer than the inbreath. His respiratory rate is set at 40, so the machine will deliver 40 breaths per minute.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. A further chest X-ray was requested. Was the plan to take a further blood gas -- is that your shorthand for an hour's time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's 1 hour after intubation so we can see what the ventilation is doing in terms of his respiratory function.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Some more sodium chloride was deemed appropriate; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think just at the top of that page, I may have commented on the fact that his heart rate had started to rise again and his blood pressure was slightly lower, so this is more fluid volume to support that circulatory volume. And then point 3, I've said that he needed another 100 micrograms per kilogram of morphine due to agitation and attempts at self extubation. So I think he was wriggling around, holding on to the tube, and without a little bit more sedation he may have pulled the tube out and required intubation again.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Hence the morphine?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: And then his background rate of morphine to give that ongoing sedation to tolerate the tube is increased to 40 micrograms per kilo per hour.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a note made at 19.20 and we know from the outset of your evidence that you've been in the hospital since the morning. Are we now approaching the end of your shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's towards the end, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And how was [Baby Q] when you handed care over to the night shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have explained what had happened over the course of the day and given some background of what the X-ray had shown and the antibiotics and their proposed reason and then that he is now ventilated. Any baby who's ventilated is going to need a review by the night-time team and they need to be mindful of blood gas tests taken overnight in case his ventilation settings need changing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: May I just remind the jury that [Dr D] the night shift, as it were, and she already gave evidence ahead of [Dr A] about her observations and her review of the X-ray that [Dr A] recommended should be taken.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For logistical reasons, we had to take that out of time sequence.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr A], did you return to look after [Baby Q] on the morning of 26 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And, Mr Murphy, could you please put up -- I think they're in the additional file, [Dr A]'s clinical notes, at J24199. Is it possible to enlarge it a little? I'm not going to go through each and every line of these notes, [Dr A], but there are a few features of it I'd like you to assist us with. In your first paragraph you include, at the final line of that paragraph, a reference to bilious aspirates.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Noted [does that say] this morning"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This morning, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll return to that in due course. If we go to the next section, the middle section of this page, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Under the F for feeds and fluids, as you told us earlier, the penultimate line there, again, is a reference to bile; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, there is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And you record that 0.5ml of dark green bile -- could you complete the reading of that sentence for me?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Sorry, yes. The sentence is:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bile: 0.5ml of dark green bile per OG tube since 08.00."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see the top of the page this is a note made at 10.25.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is this information provided to you by a third party or information discovered by you directly?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Given that it's since 08.00, I would presume that it has been observed by the member of staff looking after [Baby Q]. It may well have been left in a tube to look at. So on the desk next to the incubator, samples or aspirates are sometimes held there until they've been seen by the ward round.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is there anything within your note to assist the jury understand whether this is information provided to you verbally or information discovered by you upon inspection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This will not have been me. I wouldn't have been able to measure 0.5ml of green bile. The aspiration of the OG tube is done as regular part of the -- part of the regular care cycle, so I presume this has been since the start of the day shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we look at the bottom of this page, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: GI, which you've already educated us about, what was your GI examination (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I've said:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdomen is soft and there's increased bile per OG with right upper quadrant palpation. No palpable liver, kidney, kidney or spleen."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you help us understand the bile reference there, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This looks as though when slight pressure is placed on the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, so the bit just where the ribcage ends on the right-hand side, that there is bile showing itself into the OG tube. So just with light pressure on [Baby Q]'s abdomen, a little bit like a column of water, as I press on it I can see movement of a green liquid. Now, whether that's liquid that's remained in the OG tube since the half a millilitre was aspirated at some point after 8 o'clock, I can't say. But the fact that it's there and it's green and it's bile is a significant finding.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we go to the next page and look at the continuation of your GI note? What does the first entry inform us of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "No audible borborygmi."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's no bowel sounds, there's not the normal gurgle and flow of sounds through his abdomen. So this finding tells me that his abdomen is -- his bowel has stopped and is something called an ileus. There's no blood at the tail end seen or recorded from the -- collected in the nappy. His genitalia and anus look normal. There are small loops of bowel palpable on
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: light palpation. His umbilicus is normal. There's no flare and there's no redness.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's return to the topic of bile against the background of those observations. If we look at our -- on the paper bundle, it's page 5 using the pagination at the top right. We can perhaps read it more -- it's very small and it's been reproduced. If we put up on screen, please, Mr Murphy, the document behind tile 303.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could look to the right of the page and the entries, please, at 03.00, 06.00 and 08.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we just orientate ourselves at the column headed "NG". From memory I think it says "aspirates and vomit". It's cut off there, isn't it? If we look at that column and see what was recorded by the nurse AD at 03.00 hours and then 06.00 hours and then the nurse KB at 08.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So when describing bile -- your notes about bile, you made reference, I think, correct me if I'm wrong, to the fact that you may have been provided this information by the nurse or nurses directly or derived from the charts.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These were the charts you were referring to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What do those entries tell you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At 3 o'clock and 6 o'clock there was nothing recorded and at 8 o'clock there was 0.5ml of dark green bile.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So putting that information together with your abdominal examination as of 10.25 on 26 June, what was the picture that morning and what did that provoke you to do?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So bile generally means that the bowel is not working in its normal function and the fact that bile from the gallbladder has made its way back up to the stomach and is then being aspirated out is worthy of looking for more information and seeing what is going on with this baby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what did you do to seek out more information?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There will have been an abdominal X-ray and I may well have used a light to see if that showed any signs in his abdomen -- I forget, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If Mr Murphy could take us back to J24200. At the bottom of the page, is that the abdominal X-ray that you've just referred to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Or your notes of your consideration of the abdominal Xray, more accurately. What did you discern from that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So there is a dilated loop of bowel in the right upper quadrant. There's no other gas seen throughout the abdomen. It's essentially featureless. I then discussed with Fiona Murphy, who was the surgical registrar at Alder Hey -- the images had been transferred electronically to Alder Hey and reviewed by her and she has then contacted the neonatal unit, probably directly through to me, at approximately 1 o'clock, that there is a bed available on the intensive care unit at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next page, please, Mr Murphy, finally, page 24201.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The top of the page records your continuing communication with Alder Hey and the transfer --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Essentially, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- to Alder Hey, the fact that [Dr B] was informed.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So is it right that this was done at your instigation because of your examination and piecing together of all the information on the morning of the 26th?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. The bile led me to want to look for a cause. That dilated loop in the right upper quadrant was a significant feature and, following discussion with the surgical specialist at Alder Hey, Fiona Murphy has made the decision that she needs to see [Baby Q] and has arranged for a bed for him at intensive care.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. The final entry on this page, timed at 18.00, again by you, does this record the events, the arrival of the transport team and [Baby Q]'s transportation and the verbal handover to your colleagues at Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So this is -- yes, this is my recording of the events from about 15.30 to 18.20. There will have been some requests for a repeat chest and abdo X-ray prior to loading him into the transport incubator. And there's some other medications given prior to leaving the neonatal unit and I've given a verbal handover to the intensive care transport nurse, Lisa, and then the Badger discharge letter that you showed me earlier on has
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: been prepared for transfer, and [Baby Q]'s left the unit at 18.20 in the evening.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Which letter, my Lord, is behind our tile 310, but I don't intend to take [Dr A] to any other features of it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that just a formal document that reflects that which you've recorded and --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- told us about already?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Could you remain there and answer any further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
One moment, please, [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)

[Dr A], thank you, I'd like to go back now just to piece some of this together and ask you some further questions. I would like to start, please, with tile 103, which is your initial attendance at the unit.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just go behind that, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we scroll down, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You arrived on the unit, [Dr A], at about 09.17; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Around then, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So is it the case that whatever had taken place, it seemed a fair amount of the activity had happened already at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Whatever the nature of the vomit, that was something that was described to you, it wasn't something that you saw; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Desaturation, is that to low 60s, is that what it says?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And a minor bradycardia; do you recall who said that or do you not recall?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: I don't, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You say it may have been that the Neopuffing and the bagging was going on when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see a couple of lines below that, it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Soon returned to 100%."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Does that mean 100% saturation of oxygen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was after that, because of the requirement for some breathing support, that [Baby Q] was moved to nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And he remained on CPAP --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- at that point? Thank you. If we scroll forwards -that was at about 9.17 and if we scroll forwards to the ward round at 10.10, on to the following page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know, if we just look a little bit further down, please, on that page, if we look at on examination, OE, the first thing you have written there, [Dr A], is "settled"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We'll have a look at a couple of the features that you have included there, but is it the case that whatever had happened that you attended at 9.17, relatively rapidly, [Baby Q] was stable and settled from that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. I say that because in this case, as you know, we've seen a variety of different types of incident and a variety of different sorts of deterioration.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What we have here is an incident at 9.17 but then a relatively rapid stabilisation; would you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Looking at some of the aspects on that examination, a couple of lines down, heart sounds, they were normal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The femoral pulse was normal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Blood pressure acceptable. It's in an acceptable level, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to keep your voice up a little bit.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: I'm so sorry.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's all right. It's me that's speaking loudly, but if you keep your voice loud, we can all follow that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Will do.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The anterior fontanelle is soft?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that's the part on the skull which helps you check there's no pressure that's building up and no concern that way; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We looked at the blood gas, which was taken at this time and I'm going to ask, and I apologise that we're moving between screens, we have it in paper but I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 79 which has it on there as well. But by all means make reference to the paper, [Dr A], ladies and gentlemen, if you have it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we scroll a little bit further down the page -- there we go, thank you. If we look at the picture with the blood gas -- and
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm looking, [Dr A], at those entries for 25 June where we've got 6.58, and then an entry at 9.56, and then an entry at 11.12. So I'm looking at three entries there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And if we keep in mind your evidence on the 9.56 blood gas is that actually that was venous, not capillary.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But at 6.58, do you agree, that seems to be a good or a relatively good blood gas picture for a baby like [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: 9.56, which is a little while after the incident that you were called to, some of the readings indicate an acidosis that's taken place; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And in particular, you looked at the drop in pH down to 7.194 and the increase in carbon dioxide to 8.17 and the base excess has dropped to minus 6.6?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But bearing in mind what you were saying about the ward round at 10.10 and settled and the reading -- your examination of him then, if we look at 11.12 that actually shows an improvement then in the blood gas, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: It does.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And that's an acceptable position on the blood gas for a baby in [Baby Q]'s position; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So at this point, plainly a baby that you would want to keep under observation because you were questioning why it is that there was that incident at 9.17; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But at this point no obvious ongoing deterioration in progress that you identify?

blocks.text: Would there be any difficulty with that being read now with the doctor here?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not at all, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I've got an order, a list of witnesses coming, so I know what's next.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of [NURSE B] (read)
This is a statement by the [Nurse B], dated 31 August 2018, and it reads as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked with reference to my knowledge of [Baby Q] and in particular the date of Saturday, 25 June 2016. I have had the opportunity to read through his case notes to assist with this statement."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it care or case? It says "care" but does it mean case notes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It says...
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: A distinction without much of a difference.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The nurse confirms that she does remember [Baby Q] and that she remembers [Baby Q] was in nursery 2 on the left side by the window for some of his admission:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On Saturday, 25 June 2016, I was working a long day shift from 07.30 to 20.00 hours. I have no recollection of [Baby Q] collapsing on this shift or which nursery the collapse happened in, but it is likely to have been nursery 2 as according to records [Baby Q] had a UVC in situ and babies with these lines are in nursery 1 or 2, and Lucy Letby's notes state he was moved to nursery 1 following his deterioration.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I do not remember if I was involved directly with [Baby Q] following his deterioration. According to Nurse Letby's care notes, I spoke with [Baby Q]'s parents. I do not recall this conversation. If I were to have a detailed conversation of this nature, I would have written my own patient note in relation to it. I do not believe I have been actively involved in [Baby Q]'s care on this day."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think the next witness is Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is. That's as far as we can go.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly. We'll have the break now, it's slightly earlier than normal. We'll resume again at 1.55 if that's not inconvenient to anyone, so we'll have the hour. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
