blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, Mr Astbury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Thank you, my Lord. I recall Dr Gibbs, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you state your full name for the recording, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You've been asked along today to assist with your treatment and knowledge of a baby by the name of [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You will be aware, I am sure, that others have given evidence ahead of you, so we don't need to cover much of the ground that you've helpfully set out for us. But by way of summary, and so that you know, we have heard that [Baby Q] was born at 31 weeks and 5 days' gestation. Our understanding is that you didn't have any contact with him at that point in his life.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've noted in your statement, by way of summary, that initially [Baby Q] needed assistance with his breathing, but that improved after about 11 hours and he was placed on CPAP; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He wasn't, because of the difficulties he was having, given milk feeds initially but instead was provided with intravenous nutrition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That was given via a UVC?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have noted on the second day of life small amounts of milk feeds were introduced by a nasogastric tube into [Baby Q]'s stomach?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Although the majority continued to be given intravenously?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there a purpose for giving these small amounts of milk at an early stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's called trophic feeding and it's simply to help prime the bowel and the stomach so that when proper milk feeding starts, it tends to be better tolerated. The trophic feeding is very small amounts and for [Baby Q] it was just 0.5ml every 2 hours, once every 2 hours, and that's just to prime the gut. It won't provide much nutrition; nearly all his nutrition was being provided intravenously.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's the second day of life. By the third day of life [Baby Q] was managing without CPAP by away of ventilation; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And at that stage what does that tell us about the direction of travel as far as [Baby Q]'s well-being is concerned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That he was doing well -- and in fact even when he needed ventilating in the first 11 hours of life, roughly, and then CPAP, he didn't need supplemental oxygen, he just needed air, which again is an indication that he was doing fairly well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you first become involved with [Baby Q] when he was 4 days old?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That was a Saturday, I think, 25 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was the consultant paediatrician on call that day, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your period on call that day was from 08.00 hours on the Saturday morning right through to the same time on the Sunday; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to refer you from time to time to our sequence of events chart. I think you're familiar with that now. If I could ask Mr Murphy just to put tile 92 up, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We don't need to go behind it. That shows, through the swipe data system, you attending the NNU at 08.34 on the morning of 25 June. Would that be relatively early in your period of cover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure why I was there then.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What would your normal practice be then, coming on at 8 o'clock in those circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We'd have a handover, so myself and two registrars, the one who'd been on the night shift and the one who was starting, like me, the daytime shift, would sit down with our more junior doctors -- called SHOs, or ST1 and 2s, different terminology, and there would be two of those -- to discuss the patients' progress over the previous night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And how long would that process ordinarily take?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Between half an hour -- it should be about half an hour, sometimes it takes an hour, depending on the number of patients and the complications those patients were experiencing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We normally hold that -- we don't normally hold that handover on the neonatal unit, it's held in a room by the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: paediatric ward, which is next door to the neonatal unit, which is why I can't remember why, 7 years ago, I was on the unit at 8.30 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I don't think anyone would expect you to. We're just putting together the timeline if it assists you. We are aware that at 9.17 am that morning, about 40 minutes later, [Dr A], who was the registrar on duty, was called to see [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've seen you going into the unit. We know there isn't a record of people leaving because of the way these systems work. Do you recall whether you were still on the unit at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think I was because I would conduct the ward round on the paediatric ward on a Saturday, the registrar would conduct the ward round on the neonatal unit on a Saturday morning, and then we'd hand over to each other some time late morning after we had finished the round. So I probably was on the paediatric ward around 9 o'clock onwards.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there a division of labour for the ward round between the two units?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It varies on different days of the weekend. So on the Saturday, myself, as the consultant, would do the ward round on the paediatric ward, the registrar does the ward rounds on the neonatal unit, but then after the rounds are finished which is a variable length of time, so late morning, we discuss the patients on both sides with each other, so I would normally have been on the paediatric ward.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. We've heard from [Dr A] this morning, and we've seen his note and gone through it in some detail, but he was effectively called to see [Baby Q] following a vomit and a desaturation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we heard that one of the measures taken was to provide Neopuff to [Baby Q] to assist bringing his saturations back up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Have you refreshed your memory from [Dr A]'s note as to what he noted at that particular time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are you aware that, having been Neopuffed, in fact [Baby Q]'s oxygen saturations returned to 100% not too long thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are you aware or were you told of the incident involving [Baby Q] around 9.17 that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I should have been told and it's very likely I was told, but I might not have been told until the handover that I do with the registrar once we have finished the ward rounds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. From the notes, have you reminded yourself that in fact [Baby Q] was then placed on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having improved in the way that he did?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And although antibiotics had in fact been stopped because of his progress, they were resumed given what had happened and --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- the concerns that [Dr A] had potentially at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Now, are you aware a chest X-ray was taken of [Baby Q] that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask, please, Mr Murphy to go next to tile 135. Would you have seen that X-ray during the course of the day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's very likely I would have done. But I didn't record in the notes that I had done, so I can only say it's likely I would have done.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The purpose of the X-ray, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because [Baby Q] had had a deterioration in his condition and was struggling temporarily to breathe, but he settled down
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: after the measures that [Dr A] had taken that you've just discussed, the possibilities are he could have inhaled some gastric contents or milk, although he was on such a tiny amount of milk, but he might have inhaled some gastric contents and so the X-ray may show what we call a whiteout, a prominent white patch in one of the lungs. He might have been suffering from an infection, even though he had been treated with antibiotics and they had been stopped after the first few days -- and again infections can show shadowing changes on X-rays.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it was to check whether there were any complications that might have caused his deterioration at about 9.10 that morning.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've clearly seen the X-ray and bearing in mind those two concerns that you've expressed, did they support those concerns or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not the first one about inhaling gastric contents or having inhaled milk because there's no big whiteout.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think the jury are used to looking at these X-rays now. Obviously this is the heart (indicating).
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have that sort of shadowing, the heart-type shadowing in the middle of the lungs, or even the whole of the lung, if you've inhaled a lot of gastric contents or milk and there isn't such shadowing in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, for infection sometimes infection affecting the lungs of a small baby can just show generalised diffuse shadowing. This Xray does show some diffuse shadowing in the lungs, so you can see the ribs across each of the lungs but there's a lot of white shadowing, almost like cobwebs. We tend to call it reticulate shadowing, but really it does look like cobwebs. That can be a sign of infection. It can also be a sign that the airways have slightly closed down, not completely closed down, otherwise you get a whiteout. And that's not uncommon in small premature babies with stiff lungs. If they're getting tired and having difficulty with their breathing the lungs may look a little whiter, a bit more of this cobwebby appearance.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It doesn't quite fit with his sudden deterioration and the amount of clear secretions he was producing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Why is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because if a baby has a problem with their lungs getting stiffer and they're getting tired, gradually their breathing gets worse, they have an oxygen requirement and the amount of
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: oxygen they need increases and they gradually deteriorate. Whereas [Baby Q] had suddenly deteriorated at 9.10. So it's not in keeping with a little baby who was getting tired, with their lungs slowly closing down because they're stiff.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. We'll come to it in a moment but I think there was a point later in the day when that was the view taken with [Baby Q]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, by the evening.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Staying with our timeline for now, did you see [Baby Q] at all that morning yourself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's very likely that I did, yes. I didn't record in his notes, so I can't, it's 7 years ago, remind myself exactly what I did -- or even 2 to 3 years ago at the time I did my initial statement on him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Would you have discussed the morning's events with [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because we hand over all the patients to each other after we have each finished our ward rounds. And given that [Baby Q] had caused some concern, he would have almost certainly have been discussed first -- unless there was another baby on the unit who was presenting more problems than [Baby Q], but I can't remember if that was the case.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. I'm not going to take you to it but we've seen [Dr A]'s note, it incorporates a ward round, and [Baby Q] being examined in that sphere. So after the ward round the routine is for the registrar to discuss it with you; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, we discuss all the patients.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard that [Dr A] again saw [Baby Q] through the course of the afternoon. But did there come a point in the evening where you again became involved with [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I've been able to remind myself by looking at the notes that [Dr A] records that he had spoken to me about [Baby Q]. It is likely at some point that afternoon or evening I would have seen [Baby Q] again.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But [Dr A] was there dealing with him and I think he records in the notes that he discussed his plan for [Baby Q] with me and I agreed with that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Perhaps can we go to that note, please, just to confirm that. 197, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see the note that you are referring to, Dr Gibbs. It's further down the page, please. That's the afternoon note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the 19.20 that we're interested in and we can see a blood gas result, we can see some other notes from [Dr A], but it's the top of the second page, I think, is that which you were referring to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Discussed with Dr Gibbs. Agrees [is that] plans to electively" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With", that's the symbol for "with".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Plans to electively intubate due to worsening..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... of respiratory drive."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And 19 is the respiratory rate, which is quite low for a small premature baby like [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So you are discussing a specific plan in order to assist with [Baby Q]'s breathing; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you, according to your statement certainly, also take into account the observations through the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. His respiratory rate had been steadily slowing down from about 50 down to around about 20 by 7 o'clock in the evening.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could I ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 183, please. Have a look at that respiratory rate, doctor, if we may.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down. Thank you. We can see from midday on the 25th looking to the top left, are they the readings that you would have been seeing on the chart up until that point? We can see, up until in fact 19.00, shortly before that entry, that they'd dropped to the lowest point on the graph; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was part of the decision. Were you also aware of blood gas results for [Baby Q] through the course of the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's very likely I was because [Dr A] would have reported them to me and he does -- just before he's written he has discussed with me, he quotes the latest blood gas. He's written that in the notes, so it's very likely that would have been part of our discussion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the blood gases please: they're at tile 162. If we can scroll down, I think we can see a series of readings on the 25th, five in total, beginning, it would seem, at the end of the night shift at 6.58 and then resuming on the day shift through until 16.18 that afternoon.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Bearing in mind you have seen the observation chart with the respiration rate dropping and falling to what looks on the graph to certainly be a very low point, is there an interaction between that feature and these blood gas results?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not particularly, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you explain that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, the obvious -- the most obviously abnormal gas, and I'm going to concentrate for the moment on the carbon dioxide levels, which is this column here (indicating), was the one just before 10 o'clock in the morning. That would have been fairly shortly after [Baby Q] had been restarted on CPAP support following his deterioration around 9.10. That carbon dioxide level is outside the normal range, being abnormally high. The normal range being about 4 to 6.5. But that's a worry because that means he's struggling to breathe adequately, except an intervention had been started fairly shortly before that, the CPAP, and encouragingly, 2 hours -- no, just over an hour later, that carbon dioxide's come down to the high end of the normal range now, which is very encouraging because that shows how the CPAP is presumably helping [Baby Q] with his breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It stays down at about 6.5 here. And in fact around about sort of quarter past 4, it's at its lower level, it's still in the normal range. So the carbon dioxide levels were reasonable here and if a baby is not breathing well enough, or anyone, and the carbon dioxide level is rising abnormally high it causes acidosis, so this pH level becomes lower and lower. Yet this pH of 7.315 is a very satisfactory normal range acid level for a baby, so it's a little surprising that his breathing was getting
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: slower and slower but his blood gases actually, from late morning onwards, were normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we read across we can see in pretty well the central column it has the observation:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "CPAP still in use but only air, no requirement for additional" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, not needing any additional oxygen, which is an indication that his lungs are reasonably good, whatever the problem is, whether it's the lungs getting a little bit collapsed because he's getting tired before the CPAP or whether he had infection, it's not affecting his lungs too badly because if it was he'd need oxygen and he doesn't.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. So the elective intubation takes place, we can see that on the observations chart.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's done more for his clinical condition because you have to take many things into account. I would not intubate him because of his blood gas, but rather than the tests, you look at the patient, and given that his rate was getting slower and slower and dropping down to a very low level for a baby of his age, that was the indication to ventilate him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there a risk in allowing it to continue to fall without intubation in place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that he'd go into bad respiratory failure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay. That's why you described it as elective because it was a decision --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- a medical decision on the trend that you could observe?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Because of the way he was behaving rather than his blood gases.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Following that intubation did you see another X-ray?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's... Well, I have seen it now, yes. On that day, did I see it? I think it's likely I did because I know from one of the nursing reports later on that day that I'd been on the unit and spoken to [Baby Q]'s father, so therefore it's likely I would have seen the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I didn't write about the X-ray in the notes so I cannot be certain that I did.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having told us what you could see on the first X-ray from late morning, could I ask you to have a look at tile 217 and, in the context of everything you have told us about the lungs and the carbon dioxide level remaining acceptable, are there any changes, anything significant on this particular X-ray that was taken at 20.25 that evening?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. An obvious change is he's now got a marking of a plastic tube up here (indicating), that's his endotracheal tube, he's attached it a ventilator. But in his lungs, they're not as cobwebby looking, reticulate shadowing as before. They have opened up a little more, they are slightly better expanded, which is what you'd expect if you're now providing artificial ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But it doesn't show any signs of obvious infection, nor any signs of having inhaled gastric contents, and by this stage he'd been about 10 hours or more without any of those tiny milk feeds he was having before, so his stomach was being kept empty.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. So what you see there is consistent with a positive effect from the ventilation that had been --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- undertaken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, just to point out, if it helps the jury, because if I look at this, I think it looks rather different to the previous X-ray, and it is just the exposure. This is a more grey X-ray, the other one was a more black and white X-ray, and it's really a feature of how the radiographer took the picture. But when you compare the lung fields to the bones to the heart, that's how you can tell these lungs are clearer than on the previous X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's not in isolation, it's a comparative exercise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you had spoken to [Baby Q]'s dad later in the day --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- which caused you think that you had seen these Xrays and you had some contact with [Baby Q], perhaps --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- that wasn't in the notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- I spoke to him on the neonatal unit, so I would have been there, and I wouldn't talk to parents without checking out the patient and usually their relevant investigations, which should have been this X-ray at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But the reason I can't say I'm sure I saw that X-ray that day is because I am not quite sure what time I spoke to [Baby Q]'s father.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Perhaps if we look at the note because -have you taken that from one of the nursing notes, that feature?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, staff Nurse Davies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we can look at tile 238, please. Perhaps if we stick with the summary on the page before because these are so small. If you just go down. It's the last line:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dad visited and was updated by Dr Gibbs and by [Dr A] and helped to settle [Baby Q]."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We know the note is made -- in fact it begins at 10.29, so it would have been at some time before 10.29 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, but she doesn't say at what time the events had happened. We know they'd happened by the time she entered that note.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's that note that you rely on when you say you had spoken to dad?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You don't have any recollection of it; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct. We can also tell, though, that Staff Nurse Davies will have come on duty around about 7.30 and probably started looking after [Baby Q] from 8 o'clock in the evening onwards --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- so we can say it's some time between 8 o'clock and 10.30 that I saw his father.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can narrow it down to that extent at least?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Of course you told us that your duty was 24 hours on that particular occasion --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- or you were on standby for 24 hours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that [Baby Q] overnight continued to require only a low level of ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he didn't need high pressures and he didn't need any supplemental oxygen, he was managing on air.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard already from [Dr D], who was on duty that night and treating [Baby Q]. Are you aware that the pain relief and sedation continued through that shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I don't think -- and I can't remember for sure, but I don't think I was contacted about [Baby Q] by [Dr D] for the rest of the night. If I was, she ought to have written that in the notes and she didn't record that, so I think she didn't feel there was a need to inform me about [Baby Q], although she did have to intervene, there were some concerns about him, but not enough for [Dr D] to call me at home that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Did she, and you've commented upon this, note at 6.50, so towards the ends of the night shift, that [Baby Q] had been settled for the last 4 hours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sleeping?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She expressed some concern about a raised carbon dioxide level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, the blood gas at this time did show an abnormally high carbon dioxide level.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And are you aware that as a consequence of that, she increased the rate of breaths being given by the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and the next gas an hour later showed a much improved carbon dioxide, so [Baby Q] just needed a little more help from the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What we think had happened, if you look at the notes, is that [Baby Q] had probably gone to sleep. Before there was quite a lot of concern from Staff Nurse Davies and [Dr D], the registrar, seeing [Baby Q] that he wasn't settled and that he needed more pain relief, but then he seemed very settled and after he became settled, his blood gases deteriorated. That means it's very likely he was putting a fair bit of effort in to assist his own breathing, despite the sedation he was getting, in addition to the ventilator doing the breathing for him. Once he settled down and became much calmer, because of his sedation, the ventilator wasn't quite adequate -- providing adequate enough ventilation, which is why the carbon dioxide rose and that was resolved by just increasing the rate of the ventilator, not by needing to add any more pressure or any more oxygen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just dealing with ventilation in principle, we've heard a couple of times now that [Baby Q] became tired.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In your context does that have a particular meaning where perhaps you would become concerned? Tiredness to many of us might just seem the obvious, that with sleep one would be refreshed, but is it a different concept with [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If a patient of any age, but we'll take [Baby Q], a premature baby -- if [Baby Q] was getting tired and did have some breathing problems, then he may start going into respiratory failure. But he's having his observations done, and not just the observations by the nurses, intermittent blood tests to check his blood gases. But there's a fear if a patient who has breathing problems gets more and more tired their breathing will deteriorate. If a healthy person gets tired, they just go asleep and continue to breathe satisfactorily.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. So that's the distinction in this --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, your period of cover came to an end round about the end of [Dr D]'s shift, I would imagine, on the Sunday morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Although I think, is it right, that you reminded yourself and us in your statement that [Baby Q] was subsequently discussed with the paediatric surgical team at Alder Hey Hospital during the day of Sunday the 26th?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There was a concern he was suffering from the early stages of NEC?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And he was in fact transferred, we know, to Alder Hey that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that [Baby Q] returned to the Countess of Chester NNU 2 days later on the 28th?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When he returned, he no longer required any mechanical ventilation at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right: it was stopped whilst he was at Alder Hey Hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was he continuing to receive antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he received them for about 10 days and was kept nil by mouth, no milk into his tummy, for that period, which is standard treatment for suspected necrotising enterocolitis, NEC.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. [Baby Q] was discharged on 25 July 2016; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Anything you recall or can assist us with that stands out during the course of the period after his return to the NNU in Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, as far as I'm aware he progressed very satisfactorily. I saw him a couple of times and I've recorded my examinations of him at those times, I think about 3 July, and then the day before he went home.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. Did you also have occasion to see [Baby Q] as an outpatient?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he was followed up in my clinic, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: During his first year of life, did [Baby Q] suffer with gastro-oesophageal reflux?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a common problem in young babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did that resolve?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as I remember it resolved by about 1 to 2 years of age, which is commonly the case with troublesome gastrooesophageal reflux.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Any intervention required surgically?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not surgically. No, he did have medication to help his reflux, his regurgitation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did it also happen that [Baby Q] was believed to have a cow's milk protein intolerance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and he had to go on to a low-allergy milk to help that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Finally, Dr Gibbs, I would like to ask you, please, about a message that we have on our sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not from you, it's not to you, but it mentions you so I would like to ask you, please, what, if anything, you remember about it. It's at tile 240. It's sent by Nurse Lucy Letby to [Dr A]:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Do I need to be worried about what Dr Gibbs was asking?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's timed, as you'll see, about 22.45 on the Saturday evening. Not long after that note was made, as it would happen, by Nurse Davies. Do you recall any questioning by you, any conversations by you on the unit that might have provoked that message?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure what Staff Nurse Letby is referring to in this particular comment. I do remember that there was -- well, I had heightened concern about what was happening on the neonatal unit. I mentioned that when I was last in court about [Baby P]. At the time I saw [Baby P] just after one of his brothers had died, I was concerned because of the increasing number of unusual and unexpected deaths that happened on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This Saturday we're discussing for [Baby Q] was 2 days after [Baby O] had died, the day after [Baby P] had died, and I knew about both of those deaths. So I was worried about what was happening on the unit. So I can't remember which nurse or nurses I spoke to -- I think it was Mary Griffith, one of the staff nurses on the unit. When I knew there had been a deterioration in [Baby Q], and I'm struggling a bit because I didn't write my examination of [Baby Q] during that day, so I'm not sure what time it was, but as I've said before, I'd likely gone to the unit and had a handover with [Dr A] later on in the morning and so some time around then, probably, not in the evening -- well, not in the evening because we have got this message here, but not in the evening when Staff Nurse Davies was recording that I'd spoken to [Baby Q]'s father, earlier in the day, I remember wanting to know who had been looking after [Baby Q] at the time he deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Did the question go any further than that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I just wanted to know. I wouldn't normally want to know who's looking after patients, I'd want to know what had happened to the patient and then what had been done to remedy the situation, but because of concerns about what had been going on on our unit that had been growing I wanted to know who had been around looking after [Baby Q] at the time he deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You think -- you can't remember who it was, you think it might have been Mary Griffith?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think it was, but it could have been Staff Nurse Lappalainen and it might have been both of them.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Was it a question you asked of Nurse Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I recall, but I have to admit I can't remember exactly which nurses I spoke to.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Was there any other purpose to asking the question of the nurses that were on duty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... To convey some -- that I was concerned about what was happening, really. And I knew if I asked one nurse, having worked for so many years in Chester, but in the NHS, if you talks about a problem with one nurse on the unit it usually very quickly gets known by most of the nurses on the unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I have no more questions for you, doctor. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Just this: did you also want to check that [Baby Q] hadn't been left unattended at the time of his deterioration? Was that one of the concerns that you had?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall that being a particular concern. My concern was just to know who was looking after him at the time he deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Gibbs, that completes your evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You won't be required again. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, some more statements to read, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just give me a moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS AMY DAVIES (read)
It's a statement from Amy Davies, paediatric nurse, dated 23 March 2018. She says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am currently employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a band 6 neonatal practitioner. I was on maternity leave from March of 2015 to January 2016, although I did do a couple of shifts leading up to Christmas before I returned full-time."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Under the heading "[Baby Q]":
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have had the opportunity to read the nursing notes to assist with my memory. I remember [Baby Q]. I was present when [Baby Q] was admitted on to the unit and I think I was his designated nurse at this time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On Saturday, 25 June 2016 I worked a night shift from 19.30 hours to 08.00 hours. This particular shift does not stand out to me, but I do recall that Belinda Simcock and [Nurse E] were also working. I was the designated nurse for [Baby Q] and I cared for him in nursery 1 and, according to the care notes, I took over from Nurse Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do not remember the handover from her but can see from the notes that [Baby Q] did have a couple of issues during the day
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: that led to him being intubated. I remember that he was a bit restless and unsettled at the beginning of the shift and I did get a doctor to review him. He was, however, stable throughout the remainder of that shift and gave no cause for concern."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS KATE BISSELL (read)
Moving on, my Lord, to page 24, please, Kate Anne Bissell, in a statement dated 12 January 2018 states:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am Kate Bissell, a senior nurse (band 6) at the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Under the heading "[Baby Q]" she states:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I looked after [Baby Q] on the day he was transferred out from the unit, 26 June 2016. It was a day shift. He was a 31-week and 5-day baby. Nurse Amy Davies had been looking after [Baby Q] on the night shift and handed his care over to me on the day shift. He was day 3 or 4 of life and when I came on duty he had been vomiting and had an abdominal distension. He was nil by mouth and his nasogastric tube was on free drainage, which would be normal for a baby who we suspect has something wrong with his tummy. With premature babies we are looking out for infection of the gut and this is called necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Looking at his notes, when I aspirated his NGT there was some dark green bile, which is indicative of something wrong with the stomach. At the time in his notes I put that [Dr A], who was the registrar on duty, requested an abdominal X-ray. The X-ray was sent to the surgeons at Alder Hey and they confirmed that there looked to be something wrong, possibly a volvulus (a twist in the gut).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They said that [Baby Q] had to go over to Alder Hey for a surgical review. The rest of the shift was spent readying [Baby Q] for transfer over to Liverpool. The notes say he was transferred at 6.30 pm."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR BENJAMIN LAKIN (read)
Next at page 29 is Benjamin Lakin. He says in a statement dated 16 January 2020:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am Dr Benjamin Lakin. I was appointed as a locum consultant in paediatric critical care, which includes paediatric intensive care, at Alder Hey Children's Hospital in September 2014 with a permanent appointment in September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was admitted to Alder Hey Children's Hospital Liverpool on the afternoon of 26 June 2016. As I do not have a
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: strong recollection of [Baby Q], this statement is prepared with the support of his medical records.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit, which is the only ward at Alder Hey which cares for sick babies who require the assistance of a ventilator through a tracheal tube."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This, he explains, is a tube in the windpipe:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He was transferred from the special care baby care unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. He was borne quite early at 31 weeks' gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was transferred as there were concerns about his abdomen being distended and that his condition at the Countess of Chester had deteriorated with vomiting and lower oxygen levels, requiring him to be once again established on a ventilator. There were concerns that this could have been a condition called necrotising enterocolitis, which is a type of infection/inflammation within the bowel that is quite common in babies who are born early. In the most severe cases an operation may be required and so most usually the local team, in this case the Countess of Chester, will discuss the patient with our surgical colleagues at Alder Hey and then the baby will be transferred to this hospital, and in this case PICU, the paediatric intensive care unit, to assess the clinical situation as well as rule out any other causes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Unfortunately, I do not have any documentation that this was the case for [Baby Q]. My colleague Dr Holek(?), an experienced middle grade doctor registrar, assessed [Baby Q] when he arrived. The medical records show that [Baby Q] had deteriorated at the Countess of Chester on the morning of 25 June 2016, day 3 of life, having had an episode of vomiting, lowered oxygen levels and a distended abdomen. He had been placed on a ventilator. His feeds had been stopped with hydration maintained with fluids into a vein and antibiotics started.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This is typical treatment for any baby where there are concerns about the possibility of necrotising enterocolitis. When Dr Holek assessed [Baby Q] he found that he was stable and did not require high levels of support on the ventilator, he did not require drugs known as inotropes to support his circulation, and that his abdomen was very slightly swollen. These are all signs of a baby who is quite stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was receiving a number of drugs: he received three antibiotics (cefotaxime, metronidazole and teicoplanin) regularly into a vein -- this is a typical combination of drugs when NEC is suspected -- together with a morphine infusion,
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: that's a continuous intravenous dose, to maintain comfort on the ventilator as well as a sugar/salt drip [and he gives the concentrations] (saline and dextrose), with potassium chloride to maintain hydration.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Later, [Baby Q] also received paracetamol into a vein for pain relief and a drug called caffeine, which is commonly used in babies who are born prematurely to stimulate breathing to enable them to stop needing the ventilator. These were given through a tube, a catheter, into the vein in the umbilicus, commonly used in small babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I reviewed [Baby Q] on the evening of 26 June 2016 at 8.24 pm and was reassured to have found him to be very stable. He was assessed by our surgical colleagues on 26 June 2016 at 9.14 pm, who felt that [Baby Q] was stable but with some subtle signs suggestive of necrotising enterocolitis, with slightly low platelets at the Countess of Chester..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then he explains that's a cell in the blood responsible for clotting which can be low during times of serious infection:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... and some changes on an abdominal tummy X-ray. However, they also assessed him as being stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Our surgical colleagues reviewed [Baby Q] the next day on 27 June 2016, at 2.24 pm, and were pleased with his progress. He remained stable, his abdomen had returned to normal, and his abdominal X-ray had also normalised.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The decision was to transfer [Baby Q] back to the Countess of Chester, which is quite a common outcome as he was stable, to complete a course of antibiotics and gradually restart feeds at the end of the treatment period. This decision is led by the surgical team.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Over the course of the admission, [Baby Q] had continued to improve to the point where we were able to remove his breathing tube and thus take him off the ventilator. This is a very reassuring event and was successful on 27 June 2016 at 1.15 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was stable for the rest of the afternoon whilst we were waiting for the neonatal transfer service to transport [Baby Q] back to the Countess of Chester. During this time he remained stable and his blood gases, designed to check on waste products, which is important following extubation, were acceptable."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes Dr Lakin's statement, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR KATHERINE DAVIS (read)
Moving on, please, to page 32, a statement of Katherine Davis, dated 30 June 2020. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My name is Dr Katherine Davis. I have been employed by the Countess of Chester NHS Foundation Trust as a consultant paediatrician with an interest in epilepsy since September 2019. I am currently [Baby Q]'s named general paediatric consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He was previously under the care of Dr John Gibbs, who retired prior to my appointment. I have been asked to provide a summary of [Baby Q]'s current medical condition and a review of the MRI scan from 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have only met [Baby Q] in person once, on 5 November 2019. I have also undertaken a telephone consultation with [Baby Q]'s mum on 1 June 2020. The following information has been obtained from a review of his electronic medical notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] has been diagnosed with a mild right-sided hemiplegia [that's a weakness] by Dr John Gibbs on 10 August 2018. There have also been concerns about his social communication and development. As a result of this, [Baby Q] was discussed at a multidisciplinary meeting in November 2019. As part of this assessment he was seen by a paediatric physiotherapist, who had no concerns, and an occupational therapist in December 2019, who reported age-appropriate fine motor skills. These reports suggest that [Baby Q] has no significant impairment at present from his mild weakness.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] had an MRI scan of his head on 16 November 2018 in the Countess of Chester Hospital due to his mild right-sided weakness. This had been reported locally by consultant radiologist Dr D Enion at the Countess of Chester as normal. The opinion of a paediatric radiologist in Alder Hey has not currently been sought.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] is currently reviewed in my general paediatric clinic on a 6 to 12-monthly basis.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In summary, [Baby Q] has been diagnosed with a mild right-sided weakness and developmental delay. He remains under my care and I would expect [Baby Q] to have a normal lifespan but it will be necessary to continue to monitor his development as he grows up and to provide appropriate support as needed."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Report of DR STAVROS STIVAROS (read)
The next statement, in fact, is a report from Dr Stavros Stivaros, dated 26 October 2020, who is a specialist paediatric neuroradiologist, and provided a detailed report,
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: which we've been able to edit simply to include the summary of his findings, which are at page 45.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In his summary of findings, Dr Stivaros says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was born prematurely. Although he was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit, the clinical narrative appears to suggest he was well with no signs of respiratory distress or collapse until the morning of 25 June 2016 when he took a sudden and unexpected deviation in his clinical condition and required ventilatory support to recover.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I defer to my neonatal expert colleagues' assessment in regards to him having suffered a significant hypoxic ischaemic event at that time, but the imaging findings could be explained by such an event having occurred. The scan also needs to be taken in the context of a possible infection.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My understanding of the clinical findings and reports are that no significant infection was seen in [Baby Q], but again I defer to clinical opinion in this regard."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR HOWYADA ISAAC (read)
My Lord, finally, there's a statement from a Dr Howyada Isaac, dated 16 April 2020. Dr Isaac says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My name is Dr Howyada Isaac and I'm a registered medical practitioner and I have been employed as a consultant community paediatrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust since March 2012.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I outline my involvement with [Baby Q] as follows. [Baby Q] was referred to me by Dr Gibbs on 26 April 2018 because of maternal concerns about possible autism. There is a family history of autism. He demonstrated excellent social communication skills, which would go against a diagnosis of autism. However, he also had some atypical features, such as repetitive speech and mother-reported repetitive play, repetitive activities and behaviours. The plan was to review [Baby Q] once again when he had settled in nursery to monitor his progress within the nursery setting.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q]'s development was also assessed on 17 August 2018 and he was mildly delayed. He was functioning at an age equivalent of 18 months at a chronological age of 2 years 1 month.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was reviewed again on 13 February 2019 in clinic. From my observation, [Baby Q] presented with good social communication skills, which is not in line with a presentation of autism, but that his speech was repetitive. Due to the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: discrepancy in [Baby Q]'s presentation between home and clinic, I advised a period of watch and wait until [Baby Q] settles at nursery.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] was reviewed again on 20 November 2019. [Baby Q] continued to present with a mixed picture of his social communication skills, his language was repetitive, but he also had some spontaneous language. His eye contact was well integrated into his social overtures.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "To date, [Baby Q] has had the following assessments: (1) the Early Years Specialist Teaching Service on 22 October 2019; speech and language therapy report, March 2018 to 14 February 2019; speech and language therapy report on 2 October 2019; educational psychology report on 10 October 2019."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Isaac's conclusion:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] presents with a mixed picture with some good social communication skills, some repetitive speech, repetitive behaviours and not yet interacting with his peers, but this could be secondary to his language delay. To date [Baby Q] does not have a diagnosis of autism."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes the evidence to be read.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Evans next.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. About how long do you expect you're going to be with him?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: About half an hour, possibly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think what we'll do is start now and have a break after about quarter of an hour. Is that all right? We'll sort of split the afternoon more evenly up that way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Dr Evans. For the sake of the recording would you identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Dewi Evans.

blocks.text: Thank you. Dr Evans, I just want to deal with, as I always have done, with the various reports that you have written. Was your initial sift report dated 21 November 2017?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you then write a second report dated 25 January 2019?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Dr Evans, you move on in your 2019 report to make some observations concerning the period of time between [Baby Q]'s birth and the events at about 9.10 hours on 25 June.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So could you summarise what you took as being the relevant features of that period of time, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Before 9.10, looking at the nursing entries and also listening to the information from the local team, nursing and medical staff today, [Baby Q] wasn't quite well from the night before. It looked as if he was unable to tolerate his feeds. Now, this is not unusual in small babies. So when reviewing this note or any other notes, one's starting point is to look to the initial marker of instability or his being unwell.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, there were a couple of markers that he was unwell from what we heard from Nurse Downes on Friday and from her colleague earlier this week, sufficient for them to call [Dr D] to have a look at him. These related to his gastrointestinal system, in other words there was a bit of bile coming up, he
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: wasn't really tolerating his feeds. So that was my starting point in terms of concern there was something not quite right.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But from 9.10 something totally different happened, which cannot be explained on the basis that he was sickening for some kind of gastrointestinal problem -- and, you know, we've mentioned necrotising enterocolitis quite a lot -- because at 9.10 he vomited. Now, when he vomited, he was on virtually no oral feeds at all, and the last entry of aspiration showed nothing coming up in the tube from the night -- sorry, from the last entry of the night staff.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore he vomited and he vomited clear fluids.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you vomit because you've got some kind of intestinal obstruction, you're not going to vomit clear fluids, you have going to vomit fluid that contains bile. So there was clear fluids, that's quite clear. And also, from what we heard from [Dr A] it was profuse vomiting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: On top of that, what I also saw, which I don't think is in my report, is that Nurse Lappalainen, I think, noted "clear fluids +++". And on top of that, there was air aspirated, although it's not quite -- from the stomach, although it's not quite clear whether that air was aspirated before, during or after his Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But in addition to the vomiting he also suffered a very, very significant deterioration in that his heart rate fell below 100 and his oxygen saturation dropped to 68, which is a very, very significant fall in oxygen and not a fall I would expect simply from the fact that over the previous 12 hours he's not really establishing his feeds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I thought that we are now dealing with two separate incidents. It was not clear simply from looking at the notes -- I think I've mentioned this in other cases -- how to put it all together. It's far easier to put it together having heard the evidence from the people who were looking after [Baby Q] at the time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So anyway, so he vomited, he was resuscitated very, very promptly, his oxygenation returned to normal.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He was kept nil orally. The suspicion regarding necrotising enterocolitis was, in my opinion, perfectly reasonable: he was a prem baby, he was not tolerating feeds, there was not a lot of bile had come up, but some bile had come up. Therefore, keeping him off oral feeds was appropriate, putting him on metronidazole was appropriate, which is an antibiotic used in cases of NEC, and he was put on CPAP, which also is appropriate.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And on top of that, they did a number of blood tests which broadly were pretty satisfactory, and his blood gases returned to reasonable values later that morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But during the day he became increasingly tired and this led to his being ventilated, he was placed on ventilatory support later on Saturday the 26th, and the concerns continued, so again there was this peculiarity on the abdominal X-ray, which I have seen. So it was quite reasonable to ring the Alder Hey surgical team and he was transferred there on Sunday afternoon, in other words the following day.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the sequence, which was difficult to work out from simply reading the notes, but clearly there were two events taking place here.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. Let's, if we can, please, concentrate on the events at 09.10.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We know that, as you have said, [Baby Q] was receiving a very small amount of milk, 0.5ml every 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And there is potentially conflicting evidence on precisely what it was he vomited if one -- what is recorded and what has been said in oral evidence may be different things and it may be a question for the jury to determine where the truth lies.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: But taking the alternatives, please, Dr Evans, if a significant quantity of clear fluid was vomited what view did you come to?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I deduced was that he could not have vomited clear fluid or vomited anything at all unless some clear fluid had been placed down his nasogastric tube earlier, before 9.10. So with or without some air as well. But clearly there was enough clear fluid injected down his nasogastric tube into his stomach to make him vomit. He would only have vomited if he had quite a significant amount of fluid -- and also he would not have deteriorated in dropping his oxygen saturation and dropping his heart rate unless he'd experienced this phenomenon, which we've heard about previously, where his diaphragm had been interfered with, in other words he was unable to breathe properly because his tummy was full of liquid, and that is what led to the oxygen desaturation and led to the reduction in heart rate.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Once he vomited, that of course was nature's way of unsplinting the diaphragm and therefore it was easier for the resuscitation to be successful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. All right. What about the air? What conclusions did you come to so far as the air ++ or +++, however it was recorded?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are two options here. It could be a bit of both.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What we heard the day before yesterday was that the air was aspirated after he had had some Neopuffing. So therefore if you bag a baby, some air will get into the stomach. So that could be one of the explanations.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But having said that, there was very little Neopuffing taking place. So therefore it could well be that as well as having his clear fluid down his nasogastric tube just before 9.10, he had some air inflated into the stomach as well, and of course air and liquid, as a matter of the combined volume, would add to the stomach distension and increase the risk of diaphragmatic splinting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think you were posed various questions, is that right, to which you responded on 21 October 2021?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Part of the matters that you were asked about you have already dealt with, namely the note made by Nurse Lappalainen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But what you were also asked about were issues that had been raised by Lucy Letby in the interview.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've dealt with one of those, which is the Neopuff point. But you were also asked to comment on an assertion made by Lucy Letby in interview that vomiting can cause babies to swallow air.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it doesn't. When they vomit, they vomit liquid and air would come out if anything, so they're not going to swallow air.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as NEC and/or the possibility of NEC being responsible for any or all of the events at about 9.10 are
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: concerned, what view did you come to so far as that was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Well, I've seen an X-ray report from Professor Arthurs that says that there's one abnormality, which could or may be reflecting NEC.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: But you know, that's a radiology opinion. Given what happened to [Baby Q] after he left Chester, I don't think -- he either had very, very mild NEC or he had NEC -- or he didn't have NEC at all because he settled very, very promptly. I mean, he was sent back from Alder Hey very, very quickly. I think that if he was sickening from necrotising enterocolitis from late Friday/early Saturday morning, I don't think he'd have settled as quickly. I think the other reassuring thing is once he came back to Chester on 28 June, they were able to continue -- sorry, they were able to introduce oral feeds and he did not have any further significant gastrointestinal problems until he was sent home on 25 July.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, from the point of view of necrotising enterocolitis, they were very prompt in this case and in every case in Chester, to be fair, in suspecting the condition. I don't think it -- I'm certain it was not a factor in causing his vomiting and his deterioration at 9.10. I'm sure of that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the other option of consideration is that his bowel problem post-9.10 could be the result of the fact he was unwell and was the result of what we call ileus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What I mean by ileus is that the intestines stop working, in other words nothing works.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. Just pausing there for a second and putting that into context, we will remember what [Dr A] said this morning about listening to [Baby Q]'s bowel on the morning of the 26th, so the day after this incident, and not hearing anything.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, not hearing bowel sounds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not hearing bowel sounds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And then not hearing bowel sounds is -- you seriously have to consider this condition of ileus. He was on ventilation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As part of his ventilation he was on morphine, which is routine. But morphine will also interfere with your bowel activity, morphine can cause constipation, but it can interfere with bowel activity.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I'm not critical of his receiving morphine, but the bowel problem could be due to the effects of the collapse at 9.10 on Saturday morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Can you wait there, please, Dr Evans?

blocks.text: you will have learnt over the months that we've been together that estimates as to how long things are going to take are notoriously unreliable, but I've been told that as far as tomorrow is concerned it's unlikely to be a full day. It's our last day before the Easter break. It's anticipated that -- by 3 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Doctor --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No need to explain. As I said, your word is not your bond in that respect.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Good job!
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's always difficult because there's more than one person who's participating in the proceedings, but I'm hoping we will finish certainly by 4 o'clock tomorrow at the latest.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I will just go through with you, before we part company for the Easter break, days that we will definitely not be sitting, or part days we'll definitely not be sitting, once we come back together on Monday, 17 April. As you know, Tuesday the 18th is definitely not a sitting day. You've known about that for some time. I will just say a few words to you as well tomorrow afternoon before we have the next break. All right? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)

Mr Johnson, just this. As far as the materials that Mr Myers and Ms Clancy have put together in relation to the matter that was raised, I'm obviously not going to consider that at this stage. But if you wish to contribute to it, either when we re-assemble after the break or very shortly thereafter, you should feel free to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's a helpful document, if I may say so, in relation to considerations.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful for that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Good. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'd be grateful if we could have the opportunity for a quick visit with Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Someone will be straight down.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. 10.30 tomorrow.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Thursday, 6 April 2023)
